title: Responsible AI Governance (ISO/IEC 42001)
summary: Translate responsible-AI commitments into an operating management system with named owners, risk decisions, evidence, and continuous improvement.
overview: ISO/IEC 42001 concerns an organizational AI management system: how an organization establishes, operates, maintains, and improves its management of AI. It is not a runtime guardrail library or a claim that an individual model is harmless. Architecture contributes evidence and enforceable controls to that management system.

Treat governance as an operating loop spanning inventory, impact assessment, risk treatment, release decisions, monitoring, incidents, and change review. The exact implementation depends on organizational scope and obligations. The public ISO overview describes the standard's purpose; detailed conformity work requires the applicable standard and qualified organizational review.

production.poc: A prototype needs an owner, intended-use statement, and basic risk record. These make later decisions traceable without creating a ceremonial approval process for every experiment.
production.production: Production defines release criteria, accountable risk acceptance, evaluation evidence, supplier dependencies, and incident procedures. Controls should map to identified risks and measurable operating signals.
production.scale: At scale, maintain a current AI inventory and reuse evidence across systems while preserving system-specific context. Management review must respond to incidents, changing use, and control failures rather than merely collecting documents.

components.name: AI system inventory
components.role: Records purpose, owners, users, data, models, suppliers, and lifecycle status.

components.name: Risk and impact register
components.role: Connects foreseeable harms and affected parties to treatment decisions and accountable owners.

components.name: Control implementation
components.role: Provides technical and organizational measures with testable operating evidence.

components.name: Release governance
components.role: Reviews material changes against approved criteria and documents risk acceptance.

components.name: Monitoring and review
components.role: Feeds incidents, evaluations, and audit findings into corrective action.

flow.title: Define scope
flow.description: Identify the AI system, intended users, operating context, and responsible organizational roles.

flow.title: Assess impacts
flow.description: Examine foreseeable consequences and document assumptions, affected groups, and uncertainty.

flow.title: Select treatment
flow.description: Assign controls, acceptance criteria, owners, and evidence requirements to identified risks.

flow.title: Review release
flow.description: Evaluate test results and unresolved risks before the accountable release decision.

flow.title: Monitor operation
flow.description: Collect relevant performance, safety, access, and incident signals with escalation thresholds.

flow.title: Improve controls
flow.description: Investigate failures, verify corrective actions, and update the system's risk and use assumptions.

diagrams.title: Governance as an operating feedback loop
diagrams.code:
flowchart LR

 A --> C["Owned controls and evidence"]
 C --> R["Release decision"]
 R --> O["Operational monitoring"]
 O --> M["Management review"]

diagrams.caption: Architecture supplies evidence to recurring organizational decisions rather than treating governance as a one-time launch checklist.

useCase.title: Governing an underwriting support assistant
useCase.situation: An insurer introduces an assistant that summarizes applications for underwriters across several product lines.
useCase.problem: Teams evaluate model quality independently but lack a shared record of intended use, supplier changes, and unresolved risks.
useCase.requirement: The assistant must operate within a documented support role with accountable decisions about data, bias, reliability, and human oversight.
useCase.architecture: A system inventory links model and prompt versions to risk assessments, evaluation suites, release records, and operational monitoring.
runtime: A proposed model change triggers a scoped review of affected capabilities and the evidence needed for release.
After deployment, reviewer corrections and incidents feed the risk register and may require new tests or narrower operating limits.
useCase.failure: If monitoring shows a recurring unsupported exclusion summary, the owner restricts that feature and verifies remediation before restoring it.
useCase.impact: Measure overdue control actions, evidence freshness, unresolved risk ownership, and detection-to-remediation time. This example illustrates governance architecture and does not claim certification.

tradeoffs.benefit: Shared standards improve consistency and accountability.
tradeoffs.cost: Excessive centralization can delay low-risk changes.
Assessments depend on credible assumptions and informed judgment.

tradeoffs.benefit: Common platform controls reduce duplicate work.
tradeoffs.cost: Product-specific risks still require local evaluation.

failures.scenario: The inventory omits a shadow model integration
failures.detection: Dependency review finds unregistered inference traffic.
failures.recovery: Register the system and assess its actual data and operating scope.

failures.scenario: A control exists only on paper
failures.detection: Operational sampling cannot produce evidence that it runs.
failures.recovery: Assign remediation ownership and verify the control in practice.

mistakes.mistake: Equating a standard with a model safety guarantee
mistakes.fix: Distinguish management-system scope from system performance.
Assign accountable acceptance and corrective-action roles.
Trigger review for material changes and incidents.

whenToUse: AI systems need accountable organizational risk management.
Multiple teams share models, data, and supplier dependencies.
Release and operating decisions require traceable evidence.
whenNotToUse: The goal is a single technical safety mechanism.
A certification claim lacks the required assessment process.
Documentation is being substituted for operating controls.
checklist: Define system scope and intended use.
Verify corrective actions through operating evidence.
